newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mighty Gulf oil producers relaxed on Iraq's return.
newsitem.headline: Mighty Gulf oil producers relaxed on Iraq's return.

text.p: The oil powerhouse states of the Middle East Gulf are taking a relaxed view of the first exports of Iraqi crude in six years, Gulf analysts and officials said on Monday.

With the first cargo of Iraqi oil poised to leave the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan on Monday, Gulf governments are confident that world oil prices will stay strong despite increased supplies and that they will not lose clients to Iraq.

Saudi Arabia's Oil Minister Ali bin Ibrahim al-Nuaimi "asserted that Iraq's return to exports...had only a very limited effect on the oil market," the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported over the weekend.
"The market now is improving," SPA quoted al-Nuaimi who has ministerial control over oil policy in the world's largest petroleum producer and exporter.

The resumption of limited Iraqi crude exports under an "oil-for-food" deal between Baghdad and the United Nations has been eagerly watched by Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, United Arab Emirates (UAE) and other Gulf states who rely on petrodollars for at least three-quarters of their income.
For Riyadh, every dollar swing in the international oil prices effects the kingdom's take by $2.5 billion.
Economists predict that the government is on course to beat this year's budget revenue forecast by as much as $10 billion because of strong oil prices.

Analysts over the last three years have predicted sharp drops in oil prices as soon as Iraq emerged back onto the market even if its volumes were limited, as under the terms of the U.N. deal, to below 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) -- or less than one percent of total world oil supply.

Traders said that Kuwait, Dubai and Iran could be particularly hit by the deal since their crudes were similar in quality to those of Iraq and that refiners, particularly in the Far East and Asia, would be eager to renew ties with Baghdad.
But Kuwait oil officials dismiss this suggestion and say that state Kuwait Petroleum Corp will maintain its market share on Iraq's return.

"The dire forecasts have not materialised because of the timing. Demand is growing and will grow because of winter and non-OPEC supply has been overestimated," said an analyst based in the United Arab Emirates.

International benchmark Brent crude futures suffered a ferocious sell-off in the middle of last week on news that Iraqi oil export were to start but the market quickly recovered on signs of strong winter heating fuel demand.
Brent crude was trading at $23.70 a barrel on Monday, compared to average prices of $13-15 a barrel adopted by Gulf governments in their current budgets.

"Demand growth in the market is significant to accomodate the increase in oil production from Iraq...Steady demand growth over the past year has basically given room for Iraq coming back," an oil official in Bahrain said.
